---
title: "Facets and composition"
description: >
  Two ways to make many panels: facet one plot across a variable with shared
  or free scales, and combine separate plots into one figure with concat,
  tags, insets, and repeats.
---

```{r}
#| include: false
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.retina = 2,
  out.width = "100%",
  eval = requireNamespace("vellumplot", quietly = TRUE)
)
library(vellumplot)
```

There are two different reasons to end up with a grid of panels, and vellumplot
keeps them separate. *Faceting* takes one plot and splits it by a variable, so
every panel shares the same encodings and (by default) the same scales.
*Composition* takes several independent plots, each its own spec, and arranges
them into a single figure. Use faceting for small multiples of the same view;
use composition for a dashboard of different views.

## Faceting

`facet_wrap()` lays panels out in a ribbon wrapped to `ncol` or `nrow`.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, ncol = 3)
```

`facet_grid()` puts panels on a 2-D grid defined by a `rows ~ cols` formula,
which is the right tool when you are crossing two variables.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_grid(vs ~ am)
```

### Shared or free scales

By default position scales are shared across panels so the axes line up and
panels are comparable. When panels cover very different ranges, free them per
panel with `scales = "free_x"`, `"free_y"`, or `"free"`.

```{r}
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, scales = "free")
```

`scales = "free_y"` is sugar for the underlying `resolve_scale()` lattice,
which lets you set the policy per aesthetic directly. These two are equivalent:

```{r}
#| eval: false
vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, scales = "free_y")

vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl) |> resolve_scale(y = "independent")
```

### Long strip labels

Strip text is clipped to its strip, as in ggplot2, so a label wider than its
panel can't run into the next panel or off the page:

```{r}
regions <- data.frame(
  x = rep(1:4, 3),
  y = c(2, 3, 5, 4, 1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 3, 2, 1),
  region = rep(c(
    "Northern highlands and islands",
    "Central belt",
    "Southern uplands and the borders"
  ), each = 4)
)

p_long <- vplot(regions, width = 6, height = 2.4) |>
  mark_line(x = x, y = y) |>
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 3)
p_long
```

There are two ways out. `labeller = label_wrap_gen(width)` wraps each label
at `width` characters, and the strip grows to hold every line:

```{r}
vplot(regions, width = 6, height = 2.4) |>
  mark_line(x = x, y = y) |>
  facet_wrap(~region, ncol = 3, labeller = label_wrap_gen(18))
```

Or turn the clipping off with `theme(strip.clip = "off")` (ggplot2's values:
the default `"inherit"` and `"on"` clip, `"off"` doesn't), and let a label that
is only a little too long run past its strip.

### Independent colour, size and other legends

Colour, size and the other non-position scales are shared across panels by
default, so one legend describes the whole figure and a colour means the same
thing in every panel. When each panel has its own set of categories, or values
on very different ranges, a shared scale can waste most of the palette.
`resolve_scale()` takes those aesthetics too: `"independent"` trains the scale
in each panel from that panel's data alone, and each panel gets its own legend,
drawn beside its panel.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(gear)) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent")
```

`colour =` and `fill =` both name the colour scale; `size`, `alpha`, `shape`,
`linetype`, `linewidth` and `pattern` work the same way. Independent and shared
scales mix freely: here `hp` keeps one size legend while each panel rescales its
own colours.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = hp, size = qsec) |>
  facet_wrap(~am, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent")
```

The per-panel legends sit right of each panel by default; each column of panels
gets a legend track as wide as the widest legend in it. They follow
`theme(legend.position = )`, so `"bottom"` puts them under each panel (one
track per row of panels, for `facet_grid()` too) and `"inside"` inside each
panel, and `legend.justification` aligns them along the panel edge.

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(carb)) |>
  facet_grid(am ~ cyl, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent") |>
  theme(legend.position = "bottom")
```

To collect them in the legend area instead, give the guide a position. Each
legend is then titled with the scale title and the panel's strip text:

```{r}
#| fig-width: 8
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(gear)) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl, labeller = label_both) |>
  resolve_scale(color = "independent") |>
  guides(color = guide_legend(position = "right"))
```

The guide position `"panel"` works for a shared scale too: its one legend is
repeated beside every panel.

Because colours are no longer comparable between panels, an independent scale
suits panels that are read one at a time. An unfaceted plot has a single panel
and ignores the setting.

## Composition

To place *different* plots side by side, build each one and combine them.
`concat()` (and its friends `hconcat()` and `vconcat()`) arrange plots into a
grid; by default they collect the legends into one shared guide.

```{r}
p1 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg, color = factor(cyl))
p2 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_boxplot(x = factor(cyl), y = mpg)
p3 <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 10)

concat(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3)
```

Control the shape with `ncol`/`nrow`, the relative sizes with
`widths`/`heights`, and irregular layouts with a `design` string.
`plot_spacer()` drops an empty cell, and `wrap_plots()` takes a list of plots
when you have assembled them programmatically.

```{r}
concat(p1, p2, ncol = 1, heights = c(2, 1))
```

### Titles and tags

`compose_annotation()` adds text for the whole figure (`title`, `subtitle`,
`caption`) and tags each plot: `tag_levels = "A"` labels them A, B, C, and
`"a"`, `"1"`, `"i"` and `"I"` give the other styles. `tag_prefix` and
`tag_suffix` wrap each tag, as in `"(a)"` or `"A."`.

```{r}
concat(p1, p2, p3, ncol = 3, width = 9, height = 3.2) |>
  compose_annotation(title = "Fuel economy", tag_levels = "A")
```

Each row of plots gets a band above it as tall as its tallest tag, and the tag
sits in that band at the plot's top-left corner, so it never covers a title or
a panel. The tags are drawn with the theme's `plot.tag` element, which sets
their size, colour and `angle`; pass the composition to `theme()` to change it.
This holds for compositions that can't line up their panels too (a faceted,
polar or map cell, a `design`, insets); spacers get no tag.

```{r}
faceted <- vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~am, labeller = label_both)

concat(faceted, p3, ncol = 2, widths = c(2, 1), width = 8, height = 3.4) |>
  compose_annotation(tag_levels = "a", tag_prefix = "(", tag_suffix = ")")
```

Every composition carries its own annotation, so a nested composition can have
a title and tags of its own.

### Insets

`inset()` floats one plot over another, positioned by fractional coordinates of
a reference box. Good for an overview-plus-detail figure.

```{r}
main <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg)
mini <- vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 8)
inset(main, mini, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.45, right = 1, top = 1)
```

`align_to` chooses the reference box, as patchwork's `inset_element()` does:

* `"panel"` (the default): the base plot's panel area. In a faceted plot this
  spans all the panels, strips and gaps included.
* `"plot"`: the base plot without its title, subtitle and caption, with its axes
  and legends.
* `"full"`: the whole base cell, plot margin included.

The same fractions land in different places. Here the inset takes the top-right
quarter of the whole cell, title and margins included:

```{r}
titled <- main |> labs(title = "Weight and fuel economy")
inset(titled, mini, left = 0.5, bottom = 0.5, right = 1, top = 1, align_to = "full")
```

Before vellumplot 0.22.0 every inset was placed in the whole cell; pass
`align_to = "full"` to get that placement back. When the base is a composition
of several plots there is no single panel to align to, and insets are placed in
the whole figure.

### Sparklines

`vsparkline()` is a compact, axis-free chart of a single series, sized in
physical units (mm by default) so it reads as a *word-sized graphic*. It is a
plain `PlotSpec` — render it, or `inset()` it into a figure. Three shapes: a
`"line"` trend (with a dot on its extremes or last point), a `"bar"` column
micro-chart, and a `"winloss"` chart of equal up/down bars.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
vsparkline(cumsum(rnorm(40)), width = 60, height = 16)
```

```{r}
vsparkline(rpois(24, 6), type = "bar", color = "steelblue", width = 60, height = 16)
```

Because it is a `PlotSpec`, a sparkline drops into any composition — e.g. floated
onto a plot as a tiny trend indicator:

```{r}
spark <- vsparkline(cumsum(rnorm(40)))
inset(main, spark, left = 0.55, bottom = 0.8, right = 1, top = 1)
```

### Tables with sparklines

`vtable()` lays a data frame out as a grid of cells: ordinary columns render as
text, and a **list-column of numeric vectors** renders as a per-row sparkline.
The whole table is one vector scene, so it prints and exports like any plot —
chart-in-table without leaving the plotting pipeline.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(
  metric = c("Revenue", "Users", "Latency", "Errors"),
  latest = c(4213, 18402, 128, 37),
  change = c("+4.2%", "+1.1%", "-8ms", "-12%")
)
df$trend <- lapply(1:4, function(i) cumsum(rnorm(24)))
df$volume <- lapply(1:4, function(i) rpois(20, 6))

vtable(df, spark = list(trend = "line", volume = "bar"), row_height = 8)
```

Map a column to a `type` (`"line"`/`"bar"`/`"winloss"`) or to a builder function
for full control, e.g. `spark = list(trend = \(v) vsparkline(v, color = "steelblue"))`.

### Sparkline (and grob) callouts

`annotate("sparkline", …)` drops a sparkline at a data coordinate — a little
trend callout inside a plot. More generally, `annotate("grob", grob = …)` places
*any* vellum grob (or a `PlotSpec`) at a coordinate, sized in physical units and
anchored by `halign`/`valign`.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  annotate(
    "sparkline",
    x = 4, y = 33, values = cumsum(rnorm(30)),
    width = 32, height = 10, halign = "left"
  )
```

### Sparklines in a `gt` table

Beyond the native `vtable()`, you can add a vellum sparkline column to a
[gt](https://gt.rstudio.com) table — keeping all of gt's formatting and theming.
`gt_vsparkline()` renders a list-column of numeric vectors as inline-SVG
sparklines (HTML output).

```{r}
#| eval: !expr requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
library(gt)
set.seed(1)
df <- data.frame(metric = c("Revenue", "Users", "Latency", "Errors"))
df$trend <- lapply(1:4, function(i) cumsum(rnorm(24)))
df$volume <- lapply(1:4, function(i) rpois(20, 6))

gt(df) |>
  gt_vsparkline(trend, type = "line") |>
  gt_vsparkline(volume, type = "bar", color = "#4682b4")
```

Under the hood this uses `plot_svg()`, which turns *any* vellumplot object into a
self-contained SVG string — so the same trick embeds a chart inline in
`reactable` / `DT` cells or a Quarto callout, not just gt. `inline = TRUE` drops
the XML prolog so the fragment goes straight into a paragraph, and
`recolor = c(grey30 = "currentColor")` makes the ink follow the surrounding text
colour (so it adapts to dark mode):

```r
plot_svg(
  vsparkline(cumsum(rnorm(20)), color = "grey30"),
  inline = TRUE, recolor = c(grey30 = "currentColor")
)
```

### Repeat over a variable

`repeat_()` builds a small multiple by repeating one plot template across a set
of values, the composition-side counterpart to faceting when you want each
panel to be a fully independent plot rather than a shared-scale small multiple.

Faceting and composition also compose with each other: a faceted plot is still
a spec, so it can go straight into a `concat()`. Once your figure looks right,
send it to a file the same way as any plot, with `render_plot()` (see
**[Get started](vellumplot.html)**).

## Multi-page and batch output

`render_plot()` writes one figure to one file. Two companions handle *many*
figures at once.

`pdf_pages()` writes a list of plots into a single PDF, one plot per page — a
report or a slide deck. Pages may differ in size (each plot keeps its own
`width`/`height`), and the per-page accessibility tags (see
**[Accessibility](accessibility.html)**) are written for every page.

```r
report <- list(
  vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |> labs(title = "Weight vs mpg"),
  vplot(mtcars) |> mark_histogram(x = mpg, bins = 10) |> labs(title = "mpg")
)
pdf_pages(report, "report.pdf")
```

Given a single *faceted* plot instead of a list, `pdf_pages()` splits it into
one page per facet cell — the paged counterpart of a small-multiple grid, where
each page trains its own scales and is tagged independently:

```r
vplot(mtcars) |>
  mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg) |>
  facet_wrap(~cyl) |>
  pdf_pages("by-cylinder.pdf")
```

For a slide deck you can edit, `vellum::pptx_pages()` takes the same kind of
list and writes one PowerPoint slide per plot, as editable shapes (see
[Saving to PowerPoint](vellumplot.html#saving-to-powerpoint)):

```r
vellum::pptx_pages(report, "report.pptx")
```

`render_all()` goes the other way: a list of plots to *separate* files, rendered
across CPU cores. Each plot is one independent job, so the work parallelises
cleanly (via process forks on macOS/Linux, sequentially on Windows) and the
output is byte-identical to rendering them one by one. When the list is named,
`paths` may be a single directory and each plot lands in `<name>.png`:

```r
render_all(
  list(
    weight = vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = wt, y = mpg),
    power = vplot(mtcars) |> mark_point(x = hp, y = mpg)
  ),
  "figures/"
)
```
